section.title: Modeling Forces in the Real World

families.primary_i_can: I can draw a force diagram for an object in a real-world situation.
families.evidence_job: Identify a model that assigns a force to the wrong object or omits a real interaction.
families.intended_reasoning: Student must identify a model that assigns a force to the wrong object or omits a real interaction.
families.representation_need: Use a real evidence-bearing representation when required; secure variants must change the actual stimulus/representation, not merely surface wording.

canonical_seed.student_text:
A soccer ball is rolling right on grass after the kick is over. Which candidate force model is physically correct for the ball?
A. Weight down, normal up, friction left.
B. Weight down, normal up, a “kick force” right, friction left.
C. Only a rightward motion force.
D. Normal up and kick force right, with no weight.
canonical_seed.student_html:
A soccer ball is rolling right on grass after the kick is over. Which candidate force model is physically correct for the ball?

  1. Weight down, normal up, friction left.
  2. Weight down, normal up, a “kick force” right, friction left.
  3. Only a rightward motion force.
  4. Normal up and kick force right, with no weight.
choices: Weight down, normal up, friction left.
Weight down, normal up, a “kick force” right, friction left.
Normal up and kick force right, with no weight.
canonical_seed.answer: A — Weight down, normal up, friction left.
canonical_seed.solution_text: After contact with the foot ends, there is no kick force; weight, support, and resistive friction remain.
canonical_seed.solution_html: After contact with the foot ends, there is no kick force; weight, support, and resistive friction remain.

families.primary_i_can: I can decide whether the forces are balanced or unbalanced.
families.evidence_job: Classify balanced/unbalanced systems and compare net-force magnitude.
families.intended_reasoning: Student must classify balanced/unbalanced systems and compare net-force magnitude.
families.representation_need: Use a real evidence-bearing representation when required; secure variants must change the actual stimulus/representation, not merely surface wording.

canonical_seed.student_text:
Which case has the greatest net-force magnitude?
A. Case A: 30 N left and 30 N right
B. Case B: 18 N left and 42 N right
C. Case C: 12 N left and 22 N right
D. Cases B and C are equal
canonical_seed.student_html:
Which case has the greatest net-force magnitude?

  1. Case A: 30 N left and 30 N right
  2. Case B: 18 N left and 42 N right
  3. Case C: 12 N left and 22 N right
  4. Cases B and C are equal
choices: Case A: 30 N left and 30 N right
Case B: 18 N left and 42 N right
Case C: 12 N left and 22 N right
Cases B and C are equal
canonical_seed.answer: B — Case B: 18 N left and 42 N right
canonical_seed.solution_text: Net magnitudes: A=0 N, B=24 N, C=10 N. Case B is greatest.
canonical_seed.solution_html: Net magnitudes: A=0 N, B=24 N, C=10 N. Case B is greatest.

families.primary_i_can: I can decide whether the forces are balanced or unbalanced.
families.evidence_job: Determine net force and use it to classify balance.
families.intended_reasoning: Student must determine net force and use it to classify balance.
families.representation_need: Use a real evidence-bearing representation when required; secure variants must change the actual stimulus/representation, not merely surface wording.

canonical_seed.student_text: A floor polisher has a 96 N drive force forward and 71 N friction backward. Determine the horizontal net force and classify the forces as balanced or unbalanced.

canonical_seed.solution_text: Opposite forces subtract: 96−71=25 N forward. A nonzero net force is unbalanced.
canonical_seed.solution_html: Opposite forces subtract: 96−71=25 N forward. A nonzero net force is unbalanced.

families.primary_i_can: I can explain how the net force affects the object’s motion and critique an incorrect force explanation and revise it using physics vocabulary.
families.evidence_job: Revise an incorrect force explanation using net force and precise physics vocabulary.
families.intended_reasoning: Student must revise an incorrect force explanation using net force and precise physics vocabulary.
families.representation_need: Use a real evidence-bearing representation when required; secure variants must change the actual stimulus/representation, not merely surface wording.

canonical_seed.student_text: A student says, “The cart is moving right, so the net force must point right.” The cart is moving right but slowing. Rewrite the explanation using net force and motion vocabulary.
canonical_seed.student_html: A student says, “The cart is moving right, so the net force must point right.” The cart is moving right but slowing. Rewrite the explanation using net force and motion vocabulary.
canonical_seed.answer: Because the cart is slowing while moving right, its acceleration/change in velocity points left, so the net force points left even though its current velocity points right.
canonical_seed.solution_text: Net force determines acceleration/change in velocity, not the direction of current velocity.
canonical_seed.solution_html: Net force determines acceleration/change in velocity, not the direction of current velocity.

families.primary_i_can: I can explain how the net force affects the object’s motion and critique an incorrect force explanation and revise it using physics vocabulary.
families.evidence_job: Check whether a force model and observed motion tell a consistent story.
families.intended_reasoning: Student must check whether a force model and observed motion tell a consistent story.
families.representation_need: Use a real evidence-bearing representation when required; secure variants must change the actual stimulus/representation, not merely surface wording.

canonical_seed.student_text:
A cart’s diagram shows 55 N right and 25 N left. A motion sensor shows the cart’s rightward speed increasing. Are the model and observation consistent?
A. Yes; the 30 N net force is right, matching a rightward increase in velocity.
B. No; any moving cart must have zero net force.
C. No; the net force is 80 N left.
D. Yes; because velocity and force must always be identical quantities.
canonical_seed.student_html:
A cart’s diagram shows 55 N right and 25 N left. A motion sensor shows the cart’s rightward speed increasing. Are the model and observation consistent?

  1. Yes; the 30 N net force is right, matching a rightward increase in velocity.
  2. No; any moving cart must have zero net force.
  3. No; the net force is 80 N left.
  4. Yes; because velocity and force must always be identical quantities.
choices: Yes; the 30 N net force is right, matching a rightward increase in velocity.
No; any moving cart must have zero net force.
No; the net force is 80 N left.
Yes; because velocity and force must always be identical quantities.
canonical_seed.answer: A — Yes; the 30 N net force is right, matching a rightward increase in velocity.
canonical_seed.solution_text: The force model gives 30 N net right, which is consistent with rightward acceleration.
canonical_seed.solution_html: The force model gives 30 N net right, which is consistent with rightward acceleration.

canonical_seed.student_text: A wheeled cooler is moving right. Its diagram shows 48 N push left and 20 N rolling resistance left, with no rightward horizontal force. Predict the immediate motion change and justify.
canonical_seed.student_html: A wheeled cooler is moving right. Its diagram shows 48 N push left and 20 N rolling resistance left, with no rightward horizontal force. Predict the immediate motion change and justify.
canonical_seed.answer: It accelerates left. If it is initially moving right, it will slow first because the 68 N net force is left.
canonical_seed.solution_text: The resultant is 68 N left, so the velocity changes leftward.
canonical_seed.solution_html: The resultant is 68 N left, so the velocity changes leftward.
